teaser.text: Visa is the payment network behind a card purchase, but it is not the bank that lends the money or the shop that sells the goods. To understand its business, follow a payment through the network, then follow the fees and relationships that make the network valuable.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Visa Inc.'s base case, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear begins at $27,120 million and reaches $27,734 million in the second year. It ends at $28,310 million because incentives, routing pressure, renewals, and legal costs reduce revenue retention and margins. Incentives already grew faster than net revenue in the latest quarter. The bull starts at $29,100 million and reaches $33,984 million before ending at $39,400 million. It assumes stronger spending and durable adoption of Visa Direct, commercial products, and services, whose latest-quarter growth was strong.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Visa Inc. really make after stock pay?

paragraphs.text: Stock-based pay is added back in the cash-flow statement because it is not an immediate cash payment. It is still valuable compensation and can dilute existing owners. Visa recorded $897 million of stock-based pay in FY2025. Deducting it leaves $20,680 million of economic free cash flow, or $10.52 per diluted share.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Visa Inc. today?

paragraphs.text: At US$375.10 a share, Visa trades at 31.9 times trailing earnings. In other words, an investor pays US$31.90 for each dollar of the company’s recent profit. The forward P/E is 25.0 times because it uses forecast earnings, but that lower multiple is not automatically a bargain: reported earnings may include litigation or restructuring costs that forecasts remove.

Free cash flow is the cash left after operating the business and buying property, equipment and technology. Visa’s 3.0% free-cash-flow yield and 0.7% dividend yield mean that most of the investment case depends on future growth and share repurchases, not immediate income.

blocks.heading: How much does Visa Inc. pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise in all cases because Visa has raised them every year in the five-year record. The latest quarterly declaration was $0.67, or $2.68 annualized. The base pays $3.04 per share in the first year, then $3.36 and $3.68. Roughly 12% annual increases remain below the recent increase while preserving room for litigation and investment. The bear slows growth to $2.88, $3.04, and $3.20; the bull reaches $3.20, $3.84, and $4.48. Cash generation supports continued increases, although litigation and buybacks compete for cash.

blocks.heading: Does Visa Inc.'s dividend come from its cash?

paragraphs.text: Stock-based pay is added back in the cash-flow statement because it is not an immediate cash payment. It is still valuable compensation and can dilute existing owners. Visa recorded $897 million of stock-based pay in FY2025. Deducting it leaves $20,680 million of economic free cash flow, or $10.52 per diluted share.

Across the period, dividends and buybacks consumed almost all of real free cash flow. In the last two years, shareholder returns exceeded that year’s adjusted cash generation, so Visa used other resources as well, including debt. Acquisition spending was smaller and uneven by comparison. This pattern says that Visa saw its mature network as a cash-generating asset and chose to distribute much of the harvest.

earnings.title: Visa Inc. earnings: guidance and results
earnings.meta_description: Visa Inc.'s next results are expected October 27, 2026; see management's guidance, recent results, and what to watch.
earnings.opening: Visa Inc.'s next results are expected on October 27, 2026. The key thing to watch is whether client renewals and currency conditions still support the promised pace.
earnings.closing: The full memo also answers how Visa Inc.'s business, rivals, management and risks shape the outlook.

blocks.heading: What has Visa Inc. guided for FY2026?

paragraphs.text: Visa’s financial year ends on September 30. In July, management guided to full-year FY2026 net-revenue growth at the low end of low-teens growth and earnings-per-share growth at the low end of the mid-teens. For the fourth quarter, it expected revenue growth at the high end of low-double-digit growth and earnings growth at the low end of the mid-teens.

blocks.heading: Has Visa Inc. kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Visa promised sustained growth, disciplined expenses and regular capital returns. Buybacks increased and the diluted share count fell, while services revenue grew strongly. But acquisition effects and pricing contributed to reported growth, so a lower share count and one strong period do not prove that existing operations improved equally.

blocks.heading: How have Visa Inc.'s revenue and profit changed?

paragraphs.text: Revenue reached $11,633 million, up about 14.4%. Operating income reached $6,877 million, up about 11.3%. Net income rose 6.8% to $5,628 million, while diluted EPS increased 10.4% to $2.97. Revenue therefore grew faster than operating profit, while EPS benefited from the share count.

blocks.heading: What should Visa Inc. watch in its next results?

paragraphs.text: The forecast also assumes stable consumer spending and continued currency volatility. Visa expected contracts covering roughly 20% of payment volume to be renewed by year-end. Banks choose which network their cards use, so Visa offers client incentives—payments or discounts—to retain those relationships. In the nine months ended June 2026, those incentives reached $13.2 billion. The next forecast must show whether renewals and currency conditions still support the promised pace.

Visa recorded a $2,533 million U.S. litigation provision in FY2025 and $1,255 million during the nine months to June 2026. A provision records an estimated legal expense; payment may come later. Visa said merchants representing approximately 95% of the Visa-branded sales volume of merchants that opted out of the damages settlement had settled, but that is not 95% of every possible U.S. claim.
